name: Follicular dendritic cell
summary: A stromal cell of B-cell follicles, unrelated to the dendritic cells that activate T cells. Its long, branching processes form a mesh that holds intact antigen, coated with antibody and complement, where B cells can inspect it. It also makes CXCL13 to organise the follicle. In germinal centres it is the surface on which B cells test their antibodies.
functions: Is a stromal cell, not a white blood cell: FDCs do not come from the bone marrow but from precursor cells around blood vessels (shown in mice). They do not process antigen or activate T cells.
Captures antigen as immune complexes, using complement receptors CR1 and CR2 and the Fc receptor FcγRIIB. B cells and subcapsular sinus macrophages carry the complexes to it from the lymph.
Keeps the captured antigen on its surface, intact and not digested, for a long time, so that it can be seen by B cells over weeks.
Makes CXCL13, which draws B cells and Tfh cells into the follicle through their receptor CXCR5, and BAFF, a survival signal for B cells.

In the germinal centre light zone, offers its antigen to B cells: a B cell pulls it off the FDC surface with its antibody receptor, and the cells that bind best take up the most and so win the most help from Tfh cells.
Debated: whether antigen kept on FDCs for months is needed to maintain memory B cells and antibody levels. The long retention is well shown, but its function is less certain.
abundance: Not found in blood: FDCs stay in place in the follicles of lymph nodes, spleen, tonsils and gut lymphoid tissue. Exact numbers are hard to give because FDCs are difficult to isolate, but they are a tiny minority of cells in a follicle, outnumbered many times by B cells.
